data.name: Osaka-Style Okonomiyaki With Pork Belly
data.description: Golden cabbage pancakes have tender, fluffy centers and crisp-edged pork belly. Glossy savory-sweet sauce, creamy mayonnaise and smoky bonito flakes finish this satisfying Japanese dinner.

not_suitable_for: People with soy allergies when soy is present in the dashi, sauce or mayonnaise; check product labels

refrigerator.notes: Store pancakes without toppings when possible. Refrigerate in shallow airtight containers within 2 hours of cooking, or within 1 hour when the ambient temperature exceeds 32°C (90°F). Keep at 4°C (40°F) or below.

freezer.notes: Freeze promptly cooled, untopped pancakes individually in airtight freezer containers. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator.

storage.reheating: Reheat in a covered skillet over medium-low heat, turning once, until the center reaches 74°C (165°F). Uncover briefly to crisp the surface, then add toppings.

equipment.name: Two nonstick skillets with lids, each at least 24 cm wide
equipment.alternative: A large griddle with enough space for two pancakes and a heatproof cooking dome

items.name: green cabbage
items.notes: Edible weight after removing the tough core and damaged outer leaves.

items.name: nagaimo
items.notes: Japanese mountain yam; weigh after peeling.

items.name: dashi
items.notes: Prepared, unsalted bonito-and-kelp stock, not concentrated stock powder.

items.name: eggs
items.notes: Weigh without shells; approximately 2 large eggs.

items.name: pork belly
items.notes: Boneless, skinless edible weight; use uncured slices 2–3 mm thick, cut to fit across the pancakes.

items.name: canola oil
items.notes: Divide equally between the two skillets for shallow surface cooking.

items.name: japanese mayonnaise
items.notes: Use commercially prepared mayonnaise made with pasteurized egg.

instructions.text: Chop the cabbage into pieces about 5 mm wide and finely slice the green onions on the cutting board.
Finely grate the peeled nagaimo into the mixing bowl.
tips: Nagaimo becomes slippery and sticky when grated; use a secure grip and keep fingertips clear of the grater.

instructions.text: Whisk the flour, dashi, eggs and salt into the grated nagaimo just until no dry flour remains.

doneness_cues.visual: A thick batter with no dry flour pockets.

instructions.text: Rest the batter for 10 minutes to hydrate the flour.
Preheat both skillets over medium heat with 5 g oil in each. For a temperature-controlled griddle, use approximately 180°C (356°F).

doneness_cues.visual: The oil flows easily but does not smoke.

instructions.text: Fold the cabbage and green onions into the rested batter with the mixing spoon until lightly coated throughout.
tips: Cook immediately after folding to limit water release from the cabbage.

instructions.text: Shape half the mixture in each skillet into a pancake approximately 18 cm across and 2 cm thick, gently bringing the edges together without compressing the center.

Arrange 80 g pork belly over each pancake in a single layer with minimal overlap. Use tongs for the raw pork; wash hands and clean the tongs and any surfaces that contact raw meat before handling cooked food.
Griddle the pancakes undisturbed for about 5 minutes, until the undersides are golden and the edges hold together.

doneness_cues.tactile: A spatula slides beneath each pancake without the mixture spreading.

instructions.text: Cook the pork sides by turning each pancake with two wide spatulas, covering the skillets and reducing the heat to medium-low for about 7 minutes. Clean utensils that touched uncooked batter or pork before using them again.

doneness_cues.visual: The pork is browned and the pancake sides look set.

tips: Keep the pancakes loose and thick; pressing them squeezes out moisture and makes the centers dense.

instructions.text: Finish cooking uncovered, pork side up, for about 2 minutes. Insert the thermometer horizontally into each pancake: the egg-containing center must reach at least 71°C (160°F), and the thickest pork must reach at least 63°C (145°F). Continue over low heat if needed until both readings are reached.

doneness_cues.visual: No wet batter remains in the center; the pork has browned edges.
doneness_cues.tactile: The center feels softly springy rather than liquid.

instructions.text: Rest the cooked pancakes on serving plates for at least 3 minutes before cutting, following the required rest for the pork.
Garnish each pancake with half the okonomiyaki sauce, mayonnaise, aonori and bonito flakes, spreading the sauce across the pork and drizzling the mayonnaise over it.

troubleshooting.symptom: The outside browns before the center cooks.
troubleshooting.likely_cause: The heat is too high or the pancake is thicker than 2 cm.
troubleshooting.prevention: Keep the thickness even and reduce the heat for the covered cooking stage.
troubleshooting.fix: Cover and continue over low heat, checking every 2 minutes until the center reaches 71°C (160°F) and the pork reaches at least 63°C (145°F). Rest for 3 minutes before cutting.

troubleshooting.likely_cause: The underside has not set, the cabbage pieces are too large or the pancake lacks support.
troubleshooting.prevention: Chop the cabbage finely, wait for a firm golden underside and support the pancake with two wide spatulas.
troubleshooting.fix: Push the pieces gently together and continue cooking until set and safely cooked; cover small cracks with the finishing sauce.

chef_notes: Dry cabbage thoroughly before chopping; excess surface water thins the batter and weakens the pancake.
Grated nagaimo gives the center a light, tender texture without requiring a long batter rest.
Keep pork slices thin and mostly separate so they brown evenly against the cooking surface.

The center temperature, pork temperature and resting instructions follow the applicable egg-dish and whole-cut pork guidance from [FoodSafety.gov](https://www.foodsafety.gov/food-safety-charts/safe-minimum-internal-temperatures).
data.cultural_context: Okonomiyaki is a representative dish of Osaka and the Kansai region's flour-based food culture, with cabbage mixed into batter before griddling. It became widely recognized throughout Japan as an Osaka specialty during the late 1950s and 1960s, according to [Japan's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries](https://www.maff.go.jp/e/policies/market/kryouri/searchmenu/5798/index.html).
